claims.text: High-throughput computational thermodynamic modeling combined with experimental validation can determine melting temperature across the HEA family.
The combined approach can determine enthalpy and entropy of fusion across the HEA family.
The combined approach can determine volume change at melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
HEAs typically consist of five or more principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions.
CALPHAD or machine-learning approaches can be applied in a high-throughput manner to model HEA thermodynamic properties.
DSC and dilatometry can provide targeted experimental validation of the modeled thermodynamic properties.
Controlled atmospheric conditions prevent oxidation or contamination during modeling and testing.
Multicomponent phase equilibria and atomic interactions are the relevant structural mediator for HEA thermodynamic-property prediction.
The computational model captures multicomponent phase equilibria and atomic interactions.
Computational models predict thermodynamic properties by leveraging phase-diagram and thermodynamic-parameter databases.
Direct experimental measurements can refine and validate the computational predictions.
The combined approach will predict all specified thermodynamic properties within ±5% of experimental benchmarks.
The stated ±5% accuracy will apply across a wide range of HEA compositions.
Methods relying solely on experimental measurements are time-consuming.
Methods relying solely on computational predictions are less accurate for complex HEA systems.
The approach is expected to work well when constituent elements and applicable thermodynamic databases are well characterized.
The approach may be less accurate for systems with poorly understood interactions or metastable phases.
Significant short-range ordering or non-equilibrium phases can reduce prediction accuracy because they are challenging to model computationally.
